transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-03-20
Start time (UTC): 15:00
Duration: ~64 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Diego Santos (Redwood SE), Jude Park (Redwood CSM); Lena Cho (Orchid Head of Security), Vikram Rao (Orchid Platform), Sara Bloom (Orchid Legal), Tommy Nguyen (Orchid Cloud Ops)

Summary:
Quick security review focusing on encryption at rest/in transit, BYOK/HSM trust boundaries, key rotation, audit logs and data residency controls. Customer wants assurance that keys for PII and regulated models can be hosted in their HSMs and that Redwood's private deployment will not cause cross-border key leakage. Action items and a technical follow-up were agreed.

Topics covered:
- BYOK import vs remote HSM (VM-resident keys, envelope encryption)
- HSM vendor interoperability (PKCS#11 / KMIP)
- Key rotation, escrow and revocation flows
- Audit logs, immutable trails, and SIEM integration
- Data residency and network trust boundary mapping
- SOC 2 evidence and attestation references

--- Transcript body (timestamps approximate) ---
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. Quick roll call, and then we'll jump into the BYOK design questions.
[00:10] Lena: Hi, Lena here. We want to make sure our keys never leave our control — that's the top ask.
[00:15] Diego: Totally, and that's the heart of what we wanted to cover. We support both imported keys and remote HSM integrations; we'll run through tradeoffs.
[00:22] Vikram: Quick note, our compliance team basically requires HSM-backed keys for anything classified as regulated PII, and we need to show chain-of-custody.
[00:30] Tommy: Also interested in network flow diagrams — where the key material sees plaintext, if at all.
[00:36] Maya: Good callout. Diego, do you want to start with the envelope encryption pattern?
[00:40] Diego: Sure. So Redwood uses envelope encryption by default. Customer data is encrypted with a data key (DEK) generated inside the runtime; that DEK is itself encrypted with a master key (KEK). For BYOK we can either import your KEK into our KMS under a customer-controlled lifecycle, or we can integrate to your HSM via a remote sign/encrypt interface so the KEK actually lives in your HSM and never leaves.
[01:02] Vikram: When you say "import," does that mean the plaintext key ever touches Redwood infrastructure?
[01:07] Diego: If you use the import mechanism, there is a controlled, short-lived import flow: we take an encrypted import blob you produce, which is wrapped by our import key; the plaintext never persists. But I won't sugarcoat — import requires trust in the import process and secure erase. The more strict option is remote HSM calls where the KEK never leaves your HSM; we call the HSM to unwrap/wrap.
[01:30] Lena: How does attestation work? We need proof keys are in an HSM FIPS 140-2 level or equivalent.
[01:36] Diego: We provide attestation artifacts. For cloud HSMs (AWS CloudHSM, Azure Dedicated HSM), we can provide certificate chains and signing proof. For on-prem Thales / Luna / other HSMs we ask for attestation receipts and a signed public key. Remote attestation over TPM or HSM is supported during the onboarding handshake.
[01:52] Sara: On the legal side, we need to confirm Redwood's backup and escrow policy — we can't have copies of our KEKs in Redwood backups.
[01:59] Maya: Understood. Our standard is not to take customer KEKs into backup when BYOK is enabled. Diego, can you confirm?
[02:06] Diego: Correct. When BYOK remote HSM mode is enabled, the KEK is never exported to Redwood storage. Our backups will contain only encrypted DEKs and application metadata; there is no plaintext or key material for the KEK in our backups.
[02:20] Vikram: What about key rotation? If we rotate every 90 days, how do old DEKs remain decryptable?
[02:26] Diego: We support key versioning. DEKs are tagged with the KEK version used to encrypt them. On rotation we still retain the previous KEK versions within your HSM or through your KMS import history to decrypt old objects. If you revoke an old KEK, we can mark data as inaccessible unless you provide a key recovery path.
[02:44] Lena: And what about emergency key revocation or compromise procedures? We need a playbook.
[02:49] Diego: We'll provide a runbook. Options include immediate revocation at HSM level, rotating KEKs, and re-encrypting active DEKs in the background. We also support a forced denylist for tokens if keys are revoked so new sessions can't be authorized.
[03:05] Tommy: How do network flows look? Do any Redwood control plane services see decrypted data?
[03:11] Maya: Short answer: control plane handles metadata and orchestration; data plane is where decrypted tokens are used. For private deployments (VPC) the data plane can be deployed inside your network or your cloud account so plaintext never traverses Redwood-managed networks.
[03:28] Vikram: So with a private deployment inside our VPC, we could run the runtime and Redwood would still provide the control plane?
[03:33] Maya: Yes. The private control plane coordinates and the runtime runs in your environment — keys can stay in your HSM.
[03:39] Diego: We can also do a hybrid where the runtime runs in a dedicated Redwood-managed instance inside a peered VPC where KMS calls go to your HSM via a private network. There are latency tradeoffs but it's doable.
[03:54] Lena: Audit logs are critical. We need immutable logs for key usage and admin actions. How are those surfaced?
[04:01] Diego: We stream audit events to a customer-owned S3 bucket (or Azure Blob/GCS) using a write-once pattern. Events include key unwrap/wrap, admin changes, key import, rotation, and revocation. We can integrate with your SIEM (Splunk, Sumo?) and provide signed logs for long-term retention.
[04:17] Sara: Are those logs tamper-evident? We want a chain-of-custody for legal audits.
[04:22] Diego: We sign logs (HMAC with a rotation-protected signing key) and can provide periodic digests. For very high assurance, we also support pushing logs into an append-only ledger service or timestamping with an external timestamping authority.
[04:38] Vikram: Does Redwood keep any copy of logs?
[04:41] Maya: We retain operational traces for troubleshooting per contract, but audit logs for key events can go directly to your storage endpoint. We can negotiate retention windows per the contract.
[04:50] Tommy: On encryption in transit, I just want to confirm mTLS + anti-replay?
[04:55] Diego: Yes, all data plane traffic is mTLS; we also use per-connection nonces and standard TLS 1.3 with AEAD ciphers. For HSM connections we prefer IPsec or private VPC peering to avoid internet traversals.
[05:08] Lena: For SOC 2 artifacts: do you provide a package of control descriptions and test results?
[05:12] Maya: Yes, we have a SOC 2 Type II pack and ISO overview. We'll share the redacted report and control matrix. It includes encryption controls, key management practices, and incident response summaries.
[05:22] Sara: We still need to discuss contract language around indemnity if a key compromise is due to Redwood negligence.
[05:27] Maya: Noted — we'll loop in legal and provide our standard security schedule and liability limits; we are open to negotiation for enterprise contracts.
[05:35] Vikram: A practical question — how do you support on-prem HSMs that speak KMIP vs PKCS#11?
[05:41] Diego: We support both. Our adapter layer can talk KMIP or PKCS#11 to your HSM and expose a consistent API to the runtime. The adapter can run in your environment to avoid crossing trust boundaries.
[05:53] Lena: What about performance? We're worried about latency for generate calls if each unwrap is an HSM network hop.
[05:59] Diego: We mitigate that with DEK caching (encrypted cache) and local key caches in the runtime. We only call the HSM on key unwrap/wrap events and rotation windows. Hot-path inference uses cached DEKs encrypted under KEKs but stored in the local runtime cache with TTLs, so HSM calls are minimized.
[06:21] Vikram: Ok, so the runtime holds encrypted copies of DEKs and only the HSM does KEK operations. If the runtime is compromised, are DEKs safe?
[06:29] Diego: DEKs in local cache are encrypted under the KEK. If the runtime is compromised but the KEK remains in your HSM, the attacker cannot derive plaintext without HSM access. We also support in-memory KV cache-and-zeroization policies to reduce risk.
[06:45] Tommy: Do you support bring-your-own-HSM (BYOH) where Redwood can call into our on-prem HSM using a VPN?
[06:51] Diego: Yes. We support private network peering or site-to-site VPN to call into your HSM. The adapter can also be deployed as a container inside your network to proxy calls.
[06:59] Lena: For third-party attestation, would you accept a continuous monitoring feed from our HSM vendor?
[07:04] Maya: We can consume vendor feeds as part of the onboarding. We also provide hooks for outbound health checks and attestations.
[07:11] Sara: From a legal perspective, we want to stipulate in SOW that Redwood will not export keys and will maintain signed attestation records for onboarding.
[07:18] Maya: Noted — we'll add that as part of the security schedule draft.
[07:24] Diego: I want to flag a nuance: some models do ephemeral KV caching where model context sits in memory; that context is never written to disk by default, but if customers enable snapshotting for debugging we ensure those snapshots are encrypted at rest and encrypted with the DEK/KEK chain.
[07:40] Vikram: You're mentioning snapshots — where are they stored?
[07:43] Diego: Snapshots go to customer-specified blob storage (your S3) or to a dedicated Redwood bucket if needed, but in all BYOK flows they are encrypted and the KEK remains yours.
[07:55] Lena: Any compliance gaps we should be aware of for UK/EU residency?
[07:59] Maya: We'll map the trust boundary in a diagram: control plane (managed by Redwood) can be in Redwood regions, but data plane and key ops can be pinned to EU regions inside your VPC. We'll provide an attestation that keys never cross regions.
[08:14] Vikram: What about backups and DR — is there cross-region replication of encrypted objects?
[08:20] Diego: Replication can be configured. DEKs are region-tagged; if you require strict residency we can disable cross-region replication or replicate only to explicitly allowed regions. Keys used to encrypt replicated data must be accessible in the target region — usually a mirrored HSM setup.
[08:36] Maya: Quick check — are there any blockers on your side for running a limited pilot?
[08:40] Lena: Need legal to sign the security addendum, and need a way to test HSM connectivity without full production keys.
[08:47] Diego: We usually do test keys with a certificate-based handshake and ephemeral test KEKs for initial connectivity. Those are obviously not used for production.
[08:56] Sara: On the escrow topic — in the event Orchid loses access, do you provide an emergency key recovery service?
[09:02] Diego: We don't hold your keys; recovery depends on your HSM vendor and any escrow arrangement you negotiate. For customers who want an operator-assisted recovery, we can put a solution in place where an escrow key is held under dual-control with explicit legal triggers.
[09:19] Vikram: We need dual-control and M-of-N approvals for releases.
[09:23] Diego: We can support M-of-N workflows for key unwrapping, using the HSM's native mechanisms or a multi-sig process.
[09:31] Tommy: Operationally, we'd like to integrate key usage events into our SIEM with a high-fidelity alert for any unwrapping activity.
[09:38] Diego: We'll stream those events in near real-time and can push to your Splunk/Datadog/Sumo endpoint. We can also set up predefined alerting rules.
[09:47] Lena: Any reliance on third-party secrets managers? We want the chain to be minimal.
[09:52] Diego: Minimal chain is preferred. We don't require a third-party secrets manager if you're providing an HSM endpoint. The runtime can call the HSM directly or through the adapter. For hosted customers that don't have HSMs, we use Redwood's KMS which is FIPS-compatible.
[10:06] Maya: I'm going to summarize what Diego will send after this call — the BYOK integration diagram, HSM adapter options, and a proposed key rotation and emergency revocation playbook.
[10:16] Sara: Also please send the SOC 2 type II redacted report and the control mapping table.
[10:21] Maya: Will do. Any other questions?
[10:24] Vikram: One more: does Redwood support hardware-backed signing keys for model provenance?
[10:29] Diego: Yes, we can use HSM-resident signing keys for provenance metadata, signatures on artifacts, and model checksums.
[10:36] Lena: Are there any costs or added licensing for HSM integration?
[10:40] Maya: There may be additional engineering and egress/network costs depending on the deployment model. We'll include a pricing note in the follow-up.
[10:48] Tommy: Okay — let's talk about schedule. We aim for pilot in April with a production rollout in June if everything looks good.
[10:56] Maya: Sounds feasible. We'll propose dates in the follow-up.
[11:01] Diego: I'll add a technical deep-dive session to the calendar to work through the adapter deployment and sample calls.
[11:08] Lena: Good. Also please include an example of the signed log digest we discussed.
[11:12] Diego: Will do.
[11:15] Maya: Great. Thanks everyone. We'll send the package and set up the follow-ups.

Recap and explicit next steps (verbatim from call):
- Redwood to send BYOK integration diagram,Adapter options (PKCS#11/KMIP), and sample test keys for connectivity (Owner: Maya)
- Redwood SE to produce key rotation policy, M-of-N workflows, and SIEM integration examples (Owner: Diego)

End of transcript.
